# Paths, homotopies and the fundamental group

With Henri **Poincaré**'s *Analysis Situs* (1895) topology acquired a new kind of invariant:
not a number or a property, but a **group**. Poincaré considered closed curves (*loops*) in a
space, starting and ending at a fixed base point, and declared two loops equivalent when one can
be continuously deformed into the other. Running one loop after another is a multiplication, and
the equivalence classes form the **fundamental group** `π₁(X, x₀)`. Two spaces with different
fundamental groups cannot be homeomorphic: an algebraic difference witnesses a geometric one.

The idea of a **homotopy** — a continuous one-parameter family of maps — is itself a structural
idea in the spirit of the twentieth century: one stops asking what a map *is* and asks only what
it can be *deformed into*. Many questions turn out to depend only on the homotopy class, and the
classes carry algebraic structure that the maps themselves do not have: concatenation of paths
is not associative on the nose (the parametrisations differ), but it is associative *up to
homotopy*, and that is all a group needs.

In this file:

* the **subspace metric** on a subset `{x // A x}` (so that the circle and the disc are metric
  spaces in their own right);
* **joint continuity** of functions of two variables (needed for homotopies), with a sequential
  criterion, closure properties and a **pasting lemma** for maps defined piecewise;
* **paths** (continuous maps from the parameter line, of which only `[0, 1]` matters), their
  **concatenation** `γ ⬝ δ` and **reverse** `γ⁻¹`;
* **homotopy rel endpoints**, an equivalence relation compatible with concatenation and reverse;
* the group laws up to homotopy, all derived from one **reparametrisation lemma**;
* the **fundamental group** `π₁(X, x₀)` as a quotient of loops, an instance of the project's
  `Group` class from Part IV.

Paths are represented by functions on all of `ℝ` which are continuous everywhere; only their values
on `[0, 1]` enter the notion of homotopy. This avoids relative continuity on a subinterval: any
path on `[0, 1]` extends to the whole line by composing with the **clamp** `t ↦ max 0 (min t 1)`.

# The fundamental group

Concatenation of paths is not associative: `(γ ⬝ δ) ⬝ ε` spends half of the time on `γ`, while
`γ ⬝ (δ ⬝ ε)` spends only a quarter on it. The two paths trace out the same points in the same
order, only at different speeds — and speed is precisely what a homotopy can change. The same is
true of the constant path as an identity and of the reverse path as an inverse. Each of these
laws is an instance of the **reparametrisation lemma** of the previous file: both sides are one
path composed with two reparametrisations of `[0, 1]` that agree at the endpoints.

Passing to homotopy classes of **loops** (paths from `x₀` back to `x₀`) the laws become
equations, and Poincaré's **fundamental group** `π₁(X, x₀)` appears: an instance of the
project's `Group` class from Part IV (associativity, a left identity and left inverses suffice
there; the right-handed laws are theorems).

This is the characteristic move of algebraic topology: a space is replaced by an algebraic object
which forgets almost everything — distances, shapes, even the dimension — but keeps exactly what
survives continuous deformation.

# The circle and the local inverse of the exponential map

The circle `S¹ = {z ∈ ℂ : |z| = 1}` is wrapped around by the real line through the **exponential
map** `p(θ) = cis θ = cos θ + i sin θ`. This file collects what the lifting theory of the next file
needs about `p`, about continuity in the plane, and about uniform continuity.

* **Continuity in `ℂ`**: a sequence converges iff its real and imaginary parts do; hence complex
  multiplication, subtraction, conjugation and `cis` are continuous (jointly, where there are two
  variables).
* **The kernel of `p`**: `cis x = 1` exactly when `x ∈ 2πℤ`, so `p(a) = p(b)` iff `a − b ∈ 2πℤ`.
  Every point of the circle is `p(θ)` for some `θ`.
* **The local inverse of `p`.** On the right half of the circle the angle
  `ang w = π/2 − arccos (Im w)` is the unique angle in `[−π/2, π/2]` with `cis (ang w) = w`. It is
  **Lipschitz**: by **Jordan's inequality** (from `Basel`), a chord of the circle is at least `2/π`
  times the arc it subtends, so `|ang w − ang w'| ≤ (π/2) |w − w'|`. Two points of the circle less
  than `1` apart have their quotient `z' z̄` in the right half — the domain of `ang`.
* **Uniform continuity on the square** `[0, 1]²` for jointly continuous families — the
  Lebesgue-number lemma in the form needed for lifting, proved with Bolzano–Weierstrass.

Geometrically: over every arc shorter than a half-circle, `p` is a stack of disjoint copies of the
arc, each mapped homeomorphically — `p` is a **covering map**, and `ang` (shifted by multiples of
`2π`) gives the sheets.

# Path lifting and homotopy lifting for the exponential map

The exponential map `p(θ) = cis θ` wraps the real line around the circle; over a small arc it
looks like a stack of disjoint copies of the arc, so that `p` is a **covering map** (the notion
goes back to Poincaré and to the Riemann surfaces of the nineteenth century). The computation of
`π₁(S¹)` rests on two of its properties:

* **Path lifting.** Every path `γ` in the circle has a continuous lift `L` to the line,
  `cis (L t) = γ t` on `[0, 1]`, starting at any prescribed angle over `γ 0`; two lifts differ by a
  constant (**uniqueness**).
* **Homotopy lifting.** Every jointly continuous family `H(s, t)` of points of the circle lifts to
  a jointly continuous family of angles.

The lifts are written down explicitly. Uniform continuity (`uniform_square`, the Lebesgue-number
argument of the previous file) gives `M` such that points of the path at parameter distance
`≤ 1/M` are less than `1` apart; we say the subdivision into `M` steps is **fine**. Cutting `[0, t]`
into `M` equal steps `t_k = k t / M`, every quotient `γ(t_{k+1}) · conj γ(t_k)` lies in the right
half of the circle, where the local inverse `ang` of `p` is defined, and

  `L(t) = θ₀ + Σ_{k<M} ang (γ(t_{k+1}) · conj γ(t_k))`

is a lift: applying `cis`, the sum becomes a product which **telescopes** to `γ(t) · conj γ(0)`.
Since `ang` is Lipschitz, the formula is continuous in `t` — and, for a family `H(s, ·)`, jointly
continuous in `(s, t)`: homotopy lifting comes for free.

Uniqueness rests on the intermediate value theorem: a continuous function on `[0, 1]` with values
in `2πℤ` cannot jump, so it is constant.

# The fundamental group of the circle

A loop `γ` in the circle, starting and ending at the same point, lifts to a path `L` in the line
whose endpoints lie over the same point: `L(1) − L(0) = 2πn` for an integer `n`, the **degree**
(or **winding number**) of the loop — the number of times it winds around the origin,
counted with orientation. By uniqueness of lifts, `n` does not depend on the lift chosen.

* **Homotopy invariance.** Lifting a homotopy of loops, the degree becomes a continuous function
  of the deformation parameter with values in `ℤ` — hence constant. (We prove this for *free*
  homotopies, where the base point may move; this is what the applications in the next file
  need.)
* **Additivity.** Lifting `γ` and then `δ` from where the first lift stopped gives a lift of
  `γ ⬝ δ`, so `deg (γ ⬝ δ) = deg γ + deg δ`.
* **Surjectivity.** The loop `t ↦ cis (2πnt)` has degree `n`.
* **Injectivity.** Two loops of equal degree have lifts with the same endpoints; the straight-line
  homotopy between the lifts, pushed down to the circle, is a homotopy between the loops.

Together: **`π₁(S¹) ≅ ℤ`**, the first non-trivial fundamental group, already computed in
substance by Poincaré. The circle is the simplest space with a "hole", and the integer counts how
often a loop goes around it. Everything topological about the plane in the next file — no
retraction of the disc onto its boundary, Brouwer's fixed-point theorem, the fundamental theorem
of algebra — is a consequence of this one computation.

# No retraction of the disc onto its boundary; Brouwer's fixed-point theorem in the plane

Every continuous map of the closed disc `D² = {z : |z| ≤ 1}` into itself has a **fixed point**.
L. E. J. **Brouwer** proved this, in every dimension, in 1910–12 (the planar case was known in
equivalent forms to Poincaré and to Bohl, 1904). The theorem is the archetype of a *pure
existence* statement: it asserts that a fixed point exists without offering any way to find one,
or even to approximate one in a manner that depends continuously on the map. History has a sense
of irony: a few years later Brouwer became the founder of **intuitionism**, the philosophy of
mathematics according to which an existence claim is meaningful only when accompanied by a
construction — and he came to reject, in that spirit, the very form of his own most famous
theorem. (Constructive substitutes exist: approximate fixed points can be found, but exact ones
cannot in general be computed.) The proof below is classical through and through; `#print
axioms` will duly report `Classical.choice`.

The proof is the topological one, via the degree of the previous file.

* **The boundary of a disc map has degree zero.** If `G : D² → S¹` is continuous, the boundary
  loop `t ↦ G(cis 2πt)` is freely homotopic, through the loops `t ↦ G(s · cis 2πt)`, to the
  constant loop `G(0)`; so its degree is `0`. (The disc is contractible: its inclusion induces
  the zero map on `π₁`.)
* **No retraction.** A continuous `r : D² → S¹` fixing every boundary point would have boundary
  loop `t ↦ cis 2πt`, of degree `1 ≠ 0`. The circle is not a "continuous shadow" of the disc.
* **Brouwer.** If `f : D² → D²` had no fixed point, `G(z) = (z − f z)/|z − f z|` would be a
  continuous map `D² → S¹`; its boundary loop has degree `0`, but the homotopy
  `(e − u·f(e))/|e − u·f(e)|`, `u ∈ [0, 1]`, `e = cis 2πt`, deforms it into `t ↦ cis 2πt`, of
  degree `1` — the vector `e − u·f(e)` never vanishes, since `|u·f(e)| ≤ 1 = |e|` with equality only
  if `f(e) = e`. (Classically one builds a retraction from `f`; the homotopy avoids the explicit
  formula.)
* **Maps of non-zero degree are surjective**: a loop in the circle missing a point can be
  contracted along straight segments away from it.

# The fundamental theorem of algebra, by winding numbers

Part II proved the fundamental theorem of algebra (`C.fta`) analytically, after d'Alembert and
Argand: `|p|` attains a minimum, and at a non-root one can always go further down. Here is the
other classical proof — in substance Gauss's (1799, 1849) — now in the language of the degree.

Let `p(z) = zⁿ + aₙ₋₁zⁿ⁻¹ + ⋯ + a₀` with `n ≥ 1`, and suppose `p` has no root. Choose
`ρ = 1 + Σ |aₖ|`.

* On the circle `|z| = ρ` the leading term dominates: `|Σ aₖ zᵏ| < ρⁿ = |zⁿ|`. Hence the loops
  `t ↦ zⁿ + u · Σ aₖ zᵏ` (`z = ρ cis 2πt`, `u ∈ [0, 1]`) never pass through `0`, and after
  normalisation they deform `t ↦ cis (2πnt)`, of degree `n`, into the loop `t ↦ p(ρ cis 2πt)/|·|`.
* That loop is the boundary loop of the map `z ↦ p(ρz)/|p(ρz)|` of the disc into the circle,
  so its degree is `0` (previous file).

Thus `n = 0`, a contradiction. Topologically: a polynomial of degree `n` winds a large circle `n`
times around the origin, and a loop that winds around the origin cannot be filled in without
hitting it.

# Part VIII: Topology

From the analysis of the real line to general spaces:

1. `Metric` — metric spaces (Fréchet); ℝ and ℂ; open and closed sets; convergence; ε-δ,
   sequential and topological continuity are equivalent.
2. `Topological` — topological spaces (Hausdorff, Kuratowski); the metric topology; discrete,
   indiscrete and Sierpiński spaces; subspaces and products; the Hausdorff property.
3. `Compact` — compactness; Heine–Borel; compact ⇔ sequentially compact for metric spaces;
   continuous images; the extreme value theorem from compactness.
4. `Connected` — connectedness; intervals and ℝ are connected; continuous images; the
   intermediate value theorem from connectedness; ℝ ≇ ℝ ∖ {0}; ℚ is totally disconnected.
5. `FixedPoint` — complete metric spaces; Banach's fixed-point theorem; Brouwer's fixed-point
   theorem in dimension one.
6. `Tychonoff` — the product of two compact sets is compact (tube lemma).
7. `Vitali` — no countably additive, translation-invariant measure on all subsets of `[0, 1)`.
8. `Baire` — the Baire category theorem; ℝ is not meagre; ℝ is uncountable (third proof).
9. `CantorSet` — the Cantor set: closed, compact, empty interior, uncountable.
10. `OuterMeasure` — Lebesgue outer measure; `m*([a, b]) = b − a`.
11. `UniformConvergence` — uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous; integrals of
    uniform limits; `C[a, b]` with the sup metric is complete.
12. `PicardLindelof` — existence and uniqueness for `y' = F(t, y)` via Banach's fixed-point
    theorem; `y' = y` gives `exp`.

# Ramsey's theorem

*Complete disorder is impossible.* Frank Ramsey (1930), in a paper on the decision
problem for logic, proved that in every 2-colouring of the pairs of a sufficiently
large set there is a large **monochromatic** subset — all of whose pairs have the same
colour. In the language of parties: among any six people there are three mutual
acquaintances or three mutual strangers, and six is the least number with this
property (`R(3,3) = 6`).

We prove:

* the **finite Ramsey theorem** for graphs: for all `s, t` there is `R(s, t)` such
  that every red/blue colouring of the edges of a complete graph on `R(s, t)` vertices
  contains a red `s`-clique or a blue `t`-clique, via the Erdős–Szekeres recursion
  `R(s, t) ≤ R(s − 1, t) + R(s, t − 1)`: pick a vertex `v`; among the others, either at
  least `R(s − 1, t)` are joined to `v` in red, or at least `R(s, t − 1)` in blue;
* **`R(3, 3) = 6`**: the upper bound by the recursion, the lower bound by the
  pentagon colouring of `K₅` (edges of the 5-cycle red, diagonals blue), which has no
  monochromatic triangle — checked by `decide`;
* the **infinite Ramsey theorem**: every 2-colouring of the pairs of natural numbers
  has an infinite monochromatic set. The proof chooses a vertex `x₀`, keeps the
  infinitely many vertices joined to `x₀` in the "majority" colour `b₀`, chooses `x₁`
  among them, and so on; then the colours `bₖ` repeat infinitely often (infinite
  pigeonhole), and the corresponding `xₖ` form the monochromatic set.

*Paris–Harrington.* A seemingly innocent strengthening of the finite Ramsey theorem —
requiring the homogeneous set `H` to be *relatively large*, `|H| ≥ min H` — is still
true (it follows from the infinite Ramsey theorem by compactness), but Paris and
Harrington (1977) showed that it is **not provable in Peano arithmetic**: like
Goodstein's theorem (Part III), it was among the first natural mathematical
statements shown independent of PA. This is stated informally only.

Vertices are natural numbers; a finite vertex set is a duplicate-free list; a
colouring is a symmetric function `c : ℕ → ℕ → Bool` (`true` = red).

# Kőnig's lemma

**Kőnig's lemma** (Dénes Kőnig, 1927): *every infinite, finitely branching tree has an
infinite branch.* If a tree has nodes at every depth but each node has only finitely
many children, then one can walk from the root forever. The proof: call a node
*good* if the subtree above it is still infinite. The root is good; and a good node
has finitely many children, so not all of them can be bad (a finite union of finite
subtrees is finite) — some child is good. Walking from good node to good child gives
the branch.

*A combinatorial compactness theorem.* Kőnig's lemma is the combinatorial core of the
compactness phenomena of Part III. Applied to the tree of partial truth assignments
satisfying more and more of a countable set of propositional formulas, it gives the
**compactness theorem of propositional logic** for countable languages; conversely
compactness implies Kőnig's lemma. In reverse mathematics, Kőnig's lemma for binary
trees is the system WKL₀ and for finitely branching trees it is equivalent to
arithmetical comprehension (ACA₀).

*Non-constructive and choice.* The proof is not constructive: deciding whether a node
is good requires knowing a property of infinitely many nodes, so even for a
computable tree there may be no computable branch (Kleene). For trees whose labels
are natural numbers, as here, one can always choose the *least* good child, so no
choice beyond excluded middle is needed. For trees whose nodes have arbitrary finite
sets of children, however, Kőnig's lemma requires a weak form of the axiom of
choice — over ZF it is equivalent to countable choice for families of finite sets,
and is not a theorem of ZF alone. Our proof uses `Classical.choose`.

*Representation.* A tree is a set `T` of finite sequences of natural numbers (the
nodes; `l` is the node reached by the path `l`) closed under initial segments.
**Finitely branching**: the children `l ++ [a]` of each node have bounded labels `a`.
**Infinite**: there are nodes at every depth (for finitely branching trees this is
equivalent to having infinitely many nodes).

# Hall's marriage theorem

Given finitely many finite sets `A₀, …, A_{N−1}`, when can one choose **distinct
representatives** `f(i) ∈ Aᵢ` (a "system of distinct representatives", or, in the
classical story, marry each of `N` women to a man she likes, no man marrying twice)?
An obvious necessary condition is **Hall's condition**: any `k` of the sets together
contain at least `k` elements. Philip Hall (1935) proved that it is also sufficient.

We follow the inductive proof of Halmos and Vaughan (1950), by induction on the number
of sets.

* If every proper, non-empty subfamily `I` has *strictly* more than `|I|` elements in
  its union, match one set `A_{i₀}` to any of its elements `x`, delete `x` from all
  other sets; Hall's condition survives (each union lost at most one element but had
  one to spare).
* Otherwise some proper non-empty subfamily `I` is *critical*: its union has exactly
  `|I|` elements. Match `I` by induction (it uses up exactly its union), and match the
  rest after deleting that union from their sets; Hall's condition for the rest
  follows from Hall's condition for the rest *together with* `I`.

*Representation.* The sets live in the universe `{0, …, M−1}` and are indexed by
`{0, …, N−1}`; a family is a relation `A i x` ("`x ∈ Aᵢ`"), a subfamily is a predicate on
indices, and sizes are computed by counting (`cnt`). This "bounded universe" approach
makes all the cardinality bookkeeping a matter of simple inductions.

# Finite Ramsey from infinite Ramsey, by compactness

The finite Ramsey theorem can be obtained from the infinite one without any
counting, by a **compactness argument** — the same phenomenon as the compactness
theorem of first-order logic (Part III), here in its combinatorial guise, Kőnig's
lemma. Suppose the finite theorem failed for some `s`: for every `N` there would be a
colouring of the pairs of `{0, …, N−1}` without a monochromatic `s`-set. Arrange the
*partial* colourings without monochromatic `s`-sets into a tree (a node of depth `n`
colours the first `n` pairs, in a fixed enumeration of pairs); it is finitely
branching (two colours) and infinite (by the assumption). By Kőnig's lemma it has an
infinite branch: a colouring of *all* pairs of natural numbers without a
monochromatic `s`-set — contradicting the infinite Ramsey theorem.

This proof gives no bound at all on `N` — it is purely existential. The constructive
proof of `Ramsey` gives the bound `R(s, t) ≤ binom(s+t−2, s−1)`. The difference is
significant: for the Paris–Harrington variant (see `Ramsey`), the compactness proof
still works, but no proof in Peano arithmetic exists.

# Finite probability spaces

Probability theory began with a letter. In the summer of 1654 Blaise Pascal and Pierre
de Fermat corresponded about the *problem of points* posed by the Chevalier de Méré: how
should the stakes of an interrupted game of chance be divided? Their answer — count the
equally likely ways the game could have continued — founded the calculus of chances.
Jacob Bernoulli's *Ars Conjectandi* (1713) proved the first limit theorem, the law of
large numbers; Thomas Bayes (1763) and Pierre-Simon Laplace (*Théorie analytique des
probabilités*, 1812) turned probability into a theory of inference from evidence.

What probability *is* remains debated. For the **frequentist**, `P(A)` is the long-run
relative frequency of `A` in repeated trials — and the law of large numbers (in
`LargeNumbers`) is the theorem that makes this reading coherent. For the **Bayesian**,
`P(A)` is a rational degree of belief, revised by Bayes' theorem as evidence arrives.
The mathematics is the same: Andrei Kolmogorov's *Grundbegriffe der
Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung* (1933) axiomatised probability as a measure of total mass
`1` on a σ-algebra of events. We stay **finite**, where measure theory reduces to sums:

* a **finite probability space** is a finite list of outcomes with non-negative real
  weights summing to `1` (outcomes may repeat; their weights simply add);
* an **event** is any predicate on outcomes; `P(A)` is the total weight of outcomes in
  `A`.

We prove inclusion–exclusion `P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)`, define conditional
probability `P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)`, and prove the **law of total probability** and
**Bayes' theorem** — for a single conditioning event and for a finite partition — and
the basic facts about **independence**. All numbers are the real numbers `R` of Part II.

# Random variables, expectation and variance

A **random variable** on a finite probability space is simply a real-valued function
of the outcome. Its **expectation** `E[X] = ∑ₓ P(x) X(x)` — Huygens' *expectatio*
(*De ratiociniis in ludo aleae*, 1657), the fair price of a gamble — is linear, and its
**variance** `Var X = E[(X − E X)²]` measures its spread around the mean.

We prove linearity of expectation; `Var X = E[X²] − (E X)²`; that for **independent**
random variables `E[XY] = E[X] E[Y]` — by decomposing each variable along its finitely
many values — and hence that variances of independent (indeed of pairwise
*uncorrelated*) variables add; and the two classical tail bounds:

* **Markov's inequality** `P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X] / a` for `X ≥ 0`, `a > 0`;
* **Chebyshev's inequality** (Bienaymé 1853, Chebyshev 1867)
  `P(|X − E X| ≥ ε) ≤ Var X / ε²`.

Chebyshev's inequality turns a bound on the variance into a bound on the probability of
large deviations; it is the engine of the weak law of large numbers (next file).

# The weak law of large numbers

Jacob Bernoulli spent twenty years on what he called his *theorema aureum*, published
posthumously in the *Ars Conjectandi* (1713): in a long run of independent trials, the
relative frequency of success is, with probability as close to `1` as one wishes,
as close to the true probability of success as one wishes. It is the theorem that
links probability to observed frequencies — the mathematical backbone of the
frequentist interpretation, and of every statistical estimate.

We prove it in Chebyshev's form (1867). Repeat a finite experiment `P` independently `n`
times: the **product space** `Pⁿ` has as outcomes all lists `t = (t₀, …, t_{n−1})` of
outcomes of `P`, with weight `P(t₀) ⋯ P(t_{n−1})`. A random variable `X` on `P` gives `n`
random variables `Xᵢ(t) = X(tᵢ)` on `Pⁿ`, which are identically distributed and pairwise
independent; in particular `E[Xᵢ] = μ := E[X]`, `Var Xᵢ = σ² := Var X`, and
`E[Xᵢ Xⱼ] = μ²` for `i ≠ j`. For the sample mean `Sₙ/n = (X₀ + ⋯ + X_{n−1})/n` Bienaymé's
identity gives `Var(Sₙ/n) = σ²/n`, and Chebyshev's inequality yields

`P(|Sₙ/n − μ| ≥ ε) ≤ σ² / (n ε²) → 0`  (as `n → ∞`).

The *strong* law (almost sure convergence, Borel 1909 and Kolmogorov 1930) concerns an
infinite sequence of trials and needs measure theory; it is not treated here.

# Worked examples: the binomial distribution and the Monty Hall problem

**The binomial distribution.** A *Bernoulli trial* succeeds with probability `p` and
fails with probability `1 − p`. Repeating it `n` times independently (the product space
of `LargeNumbers`), the number of successes `Sₙ` has the binomial distribution — the
distribution Bernoulli studied in the *Ars Conjectandi*. Its mean `np` and variance
`np(1 − p)` follow at once from linearity of expectation and Bienaymé's identity, with
no binomial coefficients in sight; and the law of large numbers specialises to
Bernoulli's original theorem on relative frequencies.

**The Monty Hall problem** (Selvin 1975; made famous by Marilyn vos Savant in 1990). A
car is behind one of three doors, equally likely. You pick door `0`. The host, who knows
where the car is, opens a door you did not pick that hides no car — choosing at random
if he has a choice. He opens door `1`. Should you switch to door `2`? Bayes' theorem
says yes: the car is behind door `2` with probability `2/3`. We set up the four-outcome
probability space and compute the conditional probability exactly.

# Three natural numbers, one structure

Until now the parts of this project have stood side by side. Part I built the
von Neumann numbers `0 = ∅, 1 = {∅}, 2 = {∅, {∅}}, …` inside a model of
Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory and collected them into the set `ω`; Part II built
the Peano numbers `N` as a free-standing inductive type, generated by `zero` and
`succ`; and everywhere else Lean's own `Nat` was used, licensed by two separate
"bridge" theorems (`omega_bridge`, `N.bridge_nat`), each comparing one
construction with `Nat`. Part VII added a third, categorical, perspective: any
two *natural numbers objects* are uniquely isomorphic (`IsNNO.uniqueIso`), and
`N` and `Nat` are such objects (`peanoNatIso`).

This file makes the claim that these are *one* structure literal. We exhibit
explicit bijections

    ω  ≃  N  ≃  Nat

(between the *members* of the set `ω`, the Peano numbers, and Lean's numbers)
and prove that each preserves zero, successor, addition, multiplication and the
order — where on `ω` the operations are the purely set-theoretic `+ω` and `*ω`
defined by Dedekind's recursion theorem, and the order is inclusion `⊆`. We then
check the *coherence* of the bridges: going from `N` to `ω` and on to `Nat`
gives the same answer as Part II's direct translation, and the abstract
categorical comparison map of Part VII is, concretely, the very same function.
Finally, each of these maps is the *only* map preserving zero and successor —
Dedekind's categoricity theorem (1888), proved three times over.

Philosophically this is the precise sense in which Benacerraf's question "which
sets are the numbers?" has no answer and needs none: the three candidates are
not equal (one consists of sets of type `ZFSet`, one of inductive terms, one of
kernel-accelerated binary numerals), but they are isomorphic in exactly one
structure-preserving way, so any arithmetic statement true of one is true of the
others.

# Quotients inside the set-theoretic universe

Part II built the integers, the rationals and the reals in Lean's type theory:
`Z` is a *quotient type* of `Nat × Nat`, `Q` a quotient type of fractions. A set
theorist does the same thing differently: an integer *is* an equivalence class,
that is, a particular set of ordered pairs, and "the set of integers" is a
particular set of such classes, cut out of a power set by the axiom of
separation. This is the textbook construction of every set-theory course
(e.g. Enderton, *Elements of Set Theory*, ch. 5).

This file provides the general machinery, once and for all, for carrying out
such a construction inside Part I's ZF model and comparing the result with a
quotient type. We fix:

* a set `S` (the *representatives*, e.g. `ω × ω`) and a relation `R` between
  sets (the equivalence, e.g. `⟪a, b⟫ R ⟪c, d⟫ ↔ a +ω d = c +ω b`);
* the *class* of `p ∈ S`, `cls p = {q ∈ S | p R q}` — a set, by separation;
* the *quotient set* `{x ∈ 𝒫(S) | ∃ p ∈ S, x = cls p}` — a set, by power set and
  separation.

To compare with a quotient type `Quotient s` on some type `α`, we ask for an
*encoding* `enc : α → ZFSet` of the type-theoretic representatives as members of
`S`, hitting every member of `S` and translating `≈` into `R`. Then the quotient
type and the members of the quotient set are in canonical bijection, and
operations defined on representatives on either side correspond, as soon as they
correspond on representatives. All set-theoretic operations are defined
*without choosing representatives*: the sum of two classes `X`, `Y` is the set of
all `r ∈ S` equivalent to `p ⊕ q` for *some* `p ∈ X`, `q ∈ Y` — again just
separation.

We also need the two **projections** of a Kuratowski pair as set operations;
they are defined by union and separation, without any choice.

# The integers as a set

Part II built the integers `Z` as a quotient *type*: an integer is the class of a
formal difference `a − b` of natural numbers. Here we carry out the same
construction *inside the ZF universe of Part I*, as a set theorist would:

* a formal difference is a Kuratowski pair `⟪a, b⟫` of von Neumann naturals,
  i.e. a member of the cartesian product `ω × ω`;
* two pairs are equivalent, `⟪a, b⟫ ~ ⟪c, d⟫`, when `a +ω d = c +ω b`, using the
  set-theoretic addition `+ω` defined by the recursion theorem;
* an integer is an equivalence class — a subset of `ω × ω` — and **the set ℤ** is
  the set of all classes, separated out of `𝒫(ω × ω)`;
* sum, product and negation of classes are defined *on representatives*, using the
  set-theoretic projections of pairs and `+ω`, `*ω`, then lifted to classes by
  separation; the order is `⟪a, b⟫ ≤ ⟪c, d⟫ ↔ a +ω d ⊆ c +ω b`.

Every ingredient here is a set built from `∅` by the ZF axioms: no type of
integers is presupposed. We then prove that this set-theoretic ℤ is *the same
structure* as Part II's `Z` (and hence, by Part II's bridge, as Lean's `Int`): the
comparison map `Z → ℤ_ZF` is a bijection onto the members of the set ℤ which
preserves `0`, `1`, `+`, `−`, `·` and `≤`.

So the integers do not merely have a model in set theory "in principle": the
model is constructed, and the identification is a theorem.

With the set ℤ of `IntInSets` in hand, the rationals are built in the set-theoretic

# The real numbers as a set

Dedekind (*Stetigkeit und irrationale Zahlen*, 1872) defined a real number as a
*cut* in the rationals. In set theory a cut is simply a **subset** of ℚ, so the
set of all real numbers is cut out of the power set `𝒫(ℚ)` by separation:

    ℝ := { A ∈ 𝒫(ℚ) | A is nonempty, A ≠ ℚ, A is downward closed, A has no maximum }.

Here `ℚ` is the ZF set of rationals of `RatInSets` — so a real number is a set of
equivalence classes of pairs of (a set of equivalence classes of pairs of) von
Neumann naturals: a set, made of sets, made ultimately of nothing but `∅`.

We show that this set is in order-preserving bijection with Part II's Dedekind
cuts `Cut` (which are predicates on the *type* `Q`), and hence — composing with
Part II's isomorphism `Cut.isoR` — with Part II's Cauchy reals `R`. Under the
bijection the order of reals becomes **inclusion** of sets, and the addition of
cuts becomes a set-theoretic operation on subsets of ℚ.

We also prove the completeness of the set-theoretic reals in its purest form:
**the least upper bound of a bounded nonempty set of reals is its union.** This is
the deep reason why Dedekind's construction makes completeness easy — the supremum
is not computed but simply collected, by the axiom of union.

So ℝ literally lives in the set-theoretic universe: the "one building" of this
project has the reals on an upper floor of the same house as `∅`.

# Intuitionistic and classical logic: Glivenko's bridge

Two parts of this project formalised Gentzen's natural deduction for propositional
logic, from two different motives:

* **Part III (Logic)** studied *classical* logic: `Derives Γ φ` has the
  introduction and elimination rules plus *reductio ad absurdum*, and is sound and
  complete for truth tables.
* **Part V (Types)** studied *intuitionistic* logic through the Curry–Howard
  correspondence: `ND Γ A` has the same rules *without* reductio, and its
  derivations are exactly the typed λ-terms. There it was shown that excluded middle,
  Peirce's law and double-negation elimination are *not* intuitionistically provable.

The formulas of the two systems are separately defined inductive types (Part V's
are the simple types), but they have the same shape; we write down the evident
translation and its inverse. Then:

1. **Intuitionistic ⊆ classical.** Every intuitionistic derivation translates into a
   classical one (the rules of `ND` are among those of `Derives`). Since `A ∨ ¬A` is
   classically but not intuitionistically provable, the inclusion is strict.

2. **Glivenko's theorem** (1929). Conversely, if `φ` is classically derivable from
   `Γ`, then its *double negation* `¬¬φ` is intuitionistically derivable from `Γ`.
   Classical logic thus embeds in intuitionistic logic: what the classical
   mathematician asserts, the intuitionist can at least assert to be *irrefutable*.
   In particular a *negated* formula `¬φ` is classically provable iff it is
   intuitionistically provable, and classical and intuitionistic propositional logic
   are equally consistent.

Philosophically, Glivenko's theorem (and its first-order refinement, the
Gödel–Gentzen negative translation of 1933) is the technical core of the claim that
the dispute between Brouwer and Hilbert is not about *which* propositional
statements are consistent to assert, but about what an assertion *means*: for the
intuitionist, `A ∨ B` demands a proof of one of the disjuncts; `¬¬(A ∨ B)` only
the impossibility of refuting both — and that much classical logic never exceeds.

The proof is by induction on classical derivations; the key observation is that
double negation is a *monad* in intuitionistic logic (`A ⊢ ¬¬A`, and from `¬¬A` and
`A ⊢ ¬¬B` follows `¬¬B`), and that reductio becomes provable under `¬¬`.

# Material sets and structural sets: ZF versus ETCS

Two pictures of what a set is have competed since the 1960s.

* **Material set theory** (Zermelo, Fraenkel, von Neumann; Part I). There is one
  global membership relation; every set has members which are themselves sets, and
  one may sensibly ask whether `∅ ∈ 2` or whether `1 ∈ π`. Functions are particular
  sets: sets of ordered pairs.
* **Structural set theory** (Lawvere's ETCS, 1964; Part VII). Sets are objects of a
  category and functions are primitive arrows. An element of `X` is an arrow
  `1 → X`; a set has no hidden internal nature, and isomorphic sets are
  indistinguishable. Paul Benacerraf's *What numbers could not be* (1965) — that
  arithmetic cannot settle whether `2 = {∅, {∅}}` or `2 = {{∅}}` — is the
  structuralist's favourite argument; John Mayberry (*The Foundations of
  Mathematics in the Theory of Sets*, 2000) and William Lawvere argued, from opposite
  directions, about which picture is foundationally prior.

The two are not rivals in the way they first appear: each can be interpreted in the
other. This file makes one half of that precise inside our project. The ZF sets of
Part I together with their set-theoretic functions (sets of pairs that are
functional) form a **category** `ZFCat`. Sending a set `X` to the *type of its
members* `{z // z ∈ X}` gives a functor

    El : ZFCat ⥤ Type 1

into the category of types, which Part VII showed to be a model of ETCS (in `Type`;
the same proofs work one universe up). We prove:

* `El` is **faithful** — a set-function is determined by what it does to elements
  (extensionality of graphs) — and **full** — every type-theoretic function between
  members comes from a set (by separation inside a cartesian product). So the
  material functions are exactly the structural ones.
* `El` is **not essentially surjective**: no set has as many members as there are
  sets (Russell). The type universe contains "proper classes" such as the type
  `ZFSet` itself; the ZF universe sits inside the structural world as a full
  subcategory, not as the whole.
* `ZFCat` has a terminal object `{∅}`, binary products (the Kuratowski product
  `X × Y`), and a **natural numbers object**: `ω` with `∅` and set-successor — the
  recursion theorem of Part I is precisely the NNO property. `El` **preserves** all
  of these: it sends them to a terminal object, products and an NNO in the category
  of types.
* Hence, by Part VII's categoricity, `El ω` is *uniquely* isomorphic to Lean's `Nat`
  as an NNO — and the unique isomorphism is the concrete bridge `Omega.toNat` of
  `NatBridges`. On the natural numbers, the material and the structural foundation
  provably say the same thing.

# Unification II: countable and finite, said two ways

The previous file reconciled duplicate *arithmetic* notions. This one reconciles two
pairs of duplicate notions of *size*.

**Countability.** Part I (`Sets/Cardinality.lean`) calls a type countable when it
*injects* into `ℕ` — its members can be tagged by distinct numbers. The logic of
Part III (`Logic/FOCompleteness.lean`, `Logic/TermModel.lean`,
`Logic/NonstandardArithmetic.lean`) and Part II's uncountability of the reals
(`Numbers/Uncountable.lean`) instead say "there is a *surjection* from `ℕ`" — its
members can be listed, possibly with repetitions. For a nonempty type the two agree:
from a listing, tag each member by (a chosen) position where it occurs; from a tagging,
list the members by sending each tag to the member carrying it and every unused number
to a fixed default member. (The empty type injects into `ℕ` but is not listed by any
function `ℕ → ∅`; this is the only difference.) As consequences, **the reals are
uncountable in Part I's sense**, and the countable models of the Löwenheim–Skolem
theorem are countable in Part I's sense.

**Finiteness.** Part I (`Sets/Infinite.lean`) calls a type finite when it injects into
some `Fin n`; Part IV (`Algebra/Finite.lean`) instead *equips* a type with a census
`FiniteType`, a duplicate-free list of all its elements. A census yields an injection
(the position in the list) and conversely an injection into `Fin n` yields a census
(list the elements of `Fin n` that are hit, and replace each by its preimage). The
census size `card` is then the cardinal in Part I's sense: `card α = n` exactly when `α`
is equinumerous with `Fin n`, and `card α ≤ n` whenever `α` injects into `Fin n`.

# Unification III: ordinal notations are von Neumann ordinals

The project has two theories of ordinals that never met.

* Part III (`Logic/Ordinals.lean`) works *without sets*: an ordinal below ε₀ is a finite
  tree `ON` in Cantor normal form, `zero` or `oadd a b` read `ω^a + b`, compared by a
  purely combinatorial lexicographic order `lt`; Gentzen-style, the order is proved
  well-founded on normal notations (`NF`).
* Part I (`Sets/Ordinals.lean`) works *inside the ZF universe*: a von Neumann ordinal is a
  transitive set of transitive sets, ordered by membership `∈`; the naturals are
  `vn 0 = ∅`, `vn (n+1) = vn n ∪ {vn n}`.

We connect them by von Neumann's own recipe, *an ordinal is the set of the smaller
ordinals*: define, by well-founded recursion along Part III's well-ordering,

  `⟦x⟧ = { ⟦y⟧ : y normal, y < x }`.

The recursion is legitimate precisely because Part III proved the order well-founded
(`wellFounded_R`), and the set exists by Part I's family principle (`ofFamily`, indexed
by the type of smaller normal notations). We then prove:

* every `⟦x⟧` is a **von Neumann ordinal**;
* on normal notations the map is an **order-embedding**: `y < x ↔ ⟦y⟧ ∈ ⟦x⟧`, and it is
  **injective**;
* the **finite notations** `1 + 1 + ⋯ + 1` (i.e. `ω^0 + (ω^0 + ⋯)`) go exactly to the
  von Neumann naturals: `⟦n⟧ = vn n`;
* the notation `ω = ω^1 + 0` goes to the ZF set `ω` of `Sets/ZFSet.lean`.

So all of Part III's ordinals below ε₀ — not just those below `ω^ω` — live, with their
order, among Part I's ZF ordinals.

# Primes in the progressions 4k + 1 and 4k + 3

Euclid proved (Elements IX.20) that there are infinitely many primes: multiply the primes you
have, add one, and look at any prime factor of the result. Part II formalised that argument as
`Arith.exists_prime_ge`. This chapter opens Part XII by asking a finer question: if we sort the
odd primes by their remainder modulo 4, are there infinitely many of *each* kind?

* Primes `≡ 3 (mod 4)`: 3, 7, 11, 19, 23, 31, … Euclid's trick still works with one twist.
  A number `≡ 3 (mod 4)` cannot have only prime factors `≡ 1 (mod 4)`, since products of
  numbers `≡ 1` stay `≡ 1`. So `4·N! − 1` has a prime factor `≡ 3 (mod 4)`, and it is larger
  than `N` because every number up to `N` divides `N!`. (Textbooks use `4·p₁⋯pₖ − 1`; the
  factorial does the same job and saves us bookkeeping of a finite list of primes.)
* Primes `≡ 1 (mod 4)`: 5, 13, 17, 29, 37, … Here the naive trick fails (products of primes
  `≡ 3` can be `≡ 1`), and we need a genuinely new ingredient: the *first supplement* to
  quadratic reciprocity, proved in Part IV as `neg_one_qr_iff`. It says that `−1` is a square
  modulo an odd prime `q` exactly when `q ≡ 1 (mod 4)`. Any odd prime `q` dividing
  `(2·N!)² + 1` makes `−1` a square modulo `q`, hence `q ≡ 1 (mod 4)`, and again `q > N`.

These are the two simplest cases of **Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions**
(1837): whenever `gcd(a, m) = 1`, there are infinitely many primes `≡ a (mod m)`. Dirichlet's
proof introduced characters and L-functions, i.e. analysis, into number theory; a Euclid-style
argument exists only for special progressions (those with `a² ≡ 1 mod m`, by a theorem of
Murty). Here we stop at the two progressions modulo 4; the general theorem is proved later in
this part, in `Dirichlet`, by Dirichlet's analytic method.

# Binomial coefficients and Legendre's formula

The proof of Bertrand's postulate that Paul Erdős found in 1932, aged nineteen, is a study of
one number: the **central binomial coefficient** `C(2n, n) = (2n)! / (n!)²`, the number of ways
to choose `n` things out of `2n`. Two opposite pressures act on it.

* It is **big**: `C(2n, n)` is the largest of the `2n + 1` numbers `C(2n, k)`, which add up to
  `2²ⁿ = 4ⁿ`, so `4ⁿ / (2n + 1) ≤ C(2n, n) ≤ 4ⁿ`. We prove both bounds directly from the
  recurrence `(n + 1) · C(2n+2, n+1) = 2(2n + 1) · C(2n, n)`.
* Its **prime factors are constrained**. Writing `vₚ(m)` for the exponent of `p` in `m`,
  *Legendre's formula* (1808) computes `vₚ(n!) = ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p²⌋ + ⌊n/p³⌋ + ⋯`: among `1, …, n`
  there are `⌊n/p⌋` multiples of `p`, each contributing one factor `p`, then `⌊n/p²⌋` multiples
  of `p²` contributing one more, and so on. Hence
  `vₚ(C(2n, n)) = Σₖ (⌊2n/pᵏ⌋ − 2⌊n/pᵏ⌋)`, and each summand is `0` or `1`, and is `0` once
  `pᵏ > 2n`. Consequently **every prime power dividing `C(2n, n)` is at most `2n`**, and a prime
  `p` with `2n/3 < p ≤ n` does **not** divide `C(2n, n)` at all: it occurs twice in `(2n)!`
  (as `p` and `2p`) and once in each `n!`.

Bertrand's postulate will follow by playing these facts against each other (file `Bertrand`).

Since core Lean has no binomial coefficients, we define them by Pascal's rule and prove the
factorial formula `C(a + b, a) · a! · b! = (a + b)!`. The valuation `vₚ` is defined by repeated
division.

# The primorial bound: the product of the primes up to n is at most 4ⁿ

The **primorial** `n#` is the product of all primes `p ≤ n`: `1, 1, 2, 6, 6, 30, 30, 210, …`.
Its logarithm `θ(n) = Σ_{p ≤ n} log p` is *Chebyshev's function*, and the prime number theorem
is equivalent to `θ(n) ∼ n`. Here we prove the elementary upper bound

  `n# ≤ 4ⁿ`, i.e. `θ(n) ≤ n · log 4`,

which Erdős used in his 1932 proof of Bertrand's postulate. (Chebyshev had obtained bounds of
this kind in 1852 with more delicate estimates; the slick argument below is Erdős's.)

The proof is by induction. Even `n > 2` are not prime, so `n# = (n−1)#`. For odd `n = 2m + 1`,
every prime `p` with `m + 1 < p ≤ 2m + 1` divides `(2m+1)!` but neither `m!` nor `(m+1)!`, hence
divides `C(2m+1, m+1)`. Being distinct primes, their product divides it too, and
`C(2m+1, m+1) ≤ 4ᵐ` (it is half of `C(2m+2, m+1)`, which is at most `4^(m+1)/2`). So
`(2m+1)# ≤ (m+1)# · 4ᵐ ≤ 4^(m+1) · 4ᵐ = 4^(2m+1)`.

Along the way we set up finite products `∏_{i<B} f(i)` and a decision procedure for primality,
which the next file uses for Bertrand's postulate.

# Bertrand's postulate

In 1845 Joseph Bertrand, checking tables up to three million, conjectured that for every
`n > 1` there is a prime between `n` and `2n`. He needed it for a theorem about permutation
groups. **Chebyshev** proved it in 1852, as a by-product of his estimates showing that the
number `π(x)` of primes up to `x` is of order `x / log x`. In 1919 **Ramanujan** gave a much
shorter proof using properties of the Gamma function, and in 1932 the nineteen-year-old
**Paul Erdős** made it entirely elementary — his first paper. That is the proof formalised here.

## Erdős's argument

Suppose there is no prime `p` with `n < p ≤ 2n`. Look at `C(2n, n)` and its prime
factorisation (file `Binomial`):

* no prime factor exceeds `2n`, and by assumption none lies in `(n, 2n]`;
* none lies in `(2n/3, n]` (Erdős's observation);
* primes `p > √(2n)` occur at most once, and every prime power factor is at most `2n`.

So `C(2n, n)` is at most `(2n)^(√(2n)+1)` (for the small primes) times the product of the primes
`≤ 2n/3`, which is at most `4^(2n/3)` by the primorial bound. But `C(2n, n) ≥ 4ⁿ / (2n + 1)`.
Hence `4^(n/3) ≤ (2n + 1) · (2n)^(√(2n)+1)`. The left side grows exponentially in `n`, the
right side only like `exp(c · √n · log n)`; for `n ≥ 1152` the inequality fails (we check this
with crude but fully elementary estimates: `a + 1 ≤ 2^(a/8)` for `a = ⌊√(2n)⌋ ≥ 48`).

For `n < 1152` we exhibit primes directly: `2, 3, 5, 7, 13, 23, 43, 83, 163, 317, 631, 1259`
— each less than twice its predecessor — so every interval `(n, 2n]` with `n < 1259` contains
one of them. Primality of each is checked by the Lean kernel (by `decide`, no `native_decide`).

## Beyond Bertrand

Bertrand's postulate is a weak form of the **prime number theorem**, `π(x) ∼ x / log x`,
conjectured by Gauss and Legendre around 1800 and proved in 1896 by Hadamard and de la Vallée
Poussin using complex analysis (the zeros of the Riemann zeta function); elementary proofs were
found by Selberg and Erdős in 1949. The prime number theorem gives a prime in `(n, (1 + ε) n]`
for every `ε > 0` and large `n`; whether there is always a prime between consecutive squares
(Legendre's conjecture) is still open.

# Chebyshev's bounds: π(x) is of order x / log x

How many primes are there up to `x`? Write `π(x)` for their number. Gauss, aged fifteen, guessed
from tables (1792) that the density of primes near `x` is about `1 / log x`, so that
`π(x) ≈ x / log x`; Legendre made a similar conjecture in 1798. This is the **prime number
theorem**, `π(x) log x / x → 1`, proved only in 1896 (Hadamard, de la Vallée Poussin) with complex
analysis.

The first real progress was **Chebyshev's** (1852): with elementary means he showed that
`π(x) log x / x` stays between two positive constants (he got `0.92` and `1.11`), and deduced
Bertrand's postulate. We prove such bounds, with cruder constants, from the two facts about
`C(2n, n)` that already gave Bertrand:

* **Lower bound.** Every prime power dividing `C(2n, n)` is at most `2n`, and only primes `≤ 2n`
  occur, so `C(2n, n) ≤ (2n)^π(2n)`. With `C(2n, n) ≥ 4ⁿ / (2n + 1)` this gives
  `2ⁿ ≤ (2n)^π(2n)`, and for every `m ≥ 6`: `2^⌊m/2⌋ ≤ m^π(m)`.
* **Upper bound.** The primes in `(k, n]` each exceed `k` and their product is at most the
  primorial `n# ≤ 4ⁿ`; so `k^(π(n) − k − 1) ≤ 4ⁿ`. Choosing `k = ⌊√n⌋` yields `n^π(n) ≤ 1024ⁿ`.

Taking logarithms (the natural logarithm `log` constructed in Part II):

  `⌊m/2⌋ · log 2 ≤ π(m) · log m ≤ m · log 1024`,

i.e. `(log 2 / 2 − o(1)) · m / log m ≤ π(m) ≤ (10 log 2) · m / log m`: the order of magnitude
`m / log m` is established, though not the asymptotic constant `1`.

# Characters of finite abelian groups

To isolate the primes `p ≡ a (mod q)` among all primes, Dirichlet (1837) needed a way to pick
out one residue class by *averaging*. His device, which became one of the great organising ideas
of modern mathematics, is the **character**: a homomorphism `χ : G → ℂ` from a finite abelian
group (for him, the units modulo `q`) into the non-zero complex numbers. Characters behave like
the exponentials `e^{2πikx/n}` of Fourier analysis, and the identity Dirichlet exploited is the
**orthogonality relation**

  `Σ_χ χ(a) · χ(b)⁻¹ = |G|` if `a = b`, and `0` otherwise,

which turns the indicator of a single element into a linear combination of characters. The set
`Ĝ` of characters is itself a group, the *dual group*; this is the first instance of the duality
between a group and its characters that Pontryagin, Weyl and Tate later made central to harmonic
analysis and number theory.

The orthogonality relation rests on the fact that there are **enough** characters to tell the
elements apart. We prove this without the structure theorem for finite abelian groups, by
*extending characters one generator at a time*: if `H` is a subgroup, `g ∉ H`, and `m ≥ 1` is the
least exponent with `gᵐ ∈ H`, then every character `χ` of `H` extends to `⟨H, g⟩` in
`m` ways — choose an `m`-th root `w` of `χ(gᵐ)` and send `g` to `w·ζʲ`, `ζ` a primitive `m`-th
root of unity. Running through all these choices and using `Σ_{j<m} ζ^{jk} = m·[m ∣ k]`,
orthogonality propagates from `H` to `⟨H, g⟩`. Starting from the trivial subgroup we reach all
of `G` and obtain a list of characters satisfying orthogonality; it then follows that this list
contains *every* character, so `Ĝ` is finite, `|Ĝ| = |G|`, and both orthogonality relations hold.

The roots of unity come from the polar form of Part II: `ζ = cos (2π/m) + i sin (2π/m)`.

# The dual group: enough characters, and orthogonality

This file carries out the construction announced in `Characters`. For a finite commutative group
`G` we build, by extending characters from a subgroup `H` to the subgroup `⟨H, g⟩` generated by
`H` and one more element, a list of characters of `G` satisfying

  `Σ_χ χ(x) = (number of characters) · [x = 1]`.

From this one identity everything else follows: the characters **separate points** (for `x ≠ 1`
some `χ` has `χ(x) ≠ 1`), the list contains **every** character of `G` (a character missing from
it would be orthogonal to all of them, which the identity forbids), so the characters form a
finite type `Ĝ`, with `|Ĝ| = |G|` and the two **orthogonality relations**

  `Σ_{x ∈ G} χ(x) = |G| · [χ = 1]`,   `Σ_{χ ∈ Ĝ} χ(a) · conj χ(b) = |G| · [a = b]`.

Characters take values on the unit circle (`χ(x)^{|G|} = 1`), so `conj χ(x) = χ(x⁻¹)`.

# Orthogonality, and Dirichlet characters modulo `q`

With the dual group `Ĝ` of a finite commutative group `G` in hand (file `DualGroup`), we prove
the two **orthogonality relations** and `|Ĝ| = |G|`:

* `Σ_{x ∈ G} χ(x) = |G|` if `χ` is the trivial character, `0` otherwise;
* `Σ_{χ ∈ Ĝ} χ(a) · conj χ(b) = |G|` if `a = b`, `0` otherwise.

Then we specialise to `G = (ℤ/qℤ)ˣ`. A **Dirichlet character modulo `q`** is a character `χ` of
the units, extended to all natural numbers by `χ(n) = χ(n mod q)` when `gcd(n, q) = 1` and
`χ(n) = 0` otherwise. It is *completely multiplicative* (`χ(mn) = χ(m)χ(n)`), *periodic* with
period `q`, and bounded by `1`. For a non-trivial character the values over one period sum to
zero, and the second orthogonality relation becomes Dirichlet's **sieve for a residue class**:

  `Σ_χ conj χ(a) · χ(n) = φ(q)` if `n ≡ a (mod q)`, and `0` otherwise   (`gcd(a, q) = 1`).

This identity is what lets one count primes in the class `a` by counting primes weighted by
the characters — and the analytic behaviour of these weighted counts is governed by the
`L`-functions `L(s, χ) = Σ χ(n) n⁻ˢ`.

# Arithmetic functions: divisor sums and the von Mangoldt function

Analytic number theory studies the primes through *arithmetic functions* — functions on the
positive integers — and their *divisor sums* `Σ_{d ∣ n} f(d)`. This file sets up the small amount
of such machinery that Dirichlet's theorem needs.

* **Finite-sum bookkeeping.** Interchanging double sums; summing over the multiples of `d` up
  to `N` (they are `d, 2d, …, ⌊N/d⌋ d`); and the identity behind every later estimate,

    `Σ_{n ≤ N} Σ_{d ∣ n} F(d, n/d) = Σ_{d ≤ N} Σ_{m ≤ N/d} F(d, m)`,

  which simply counts the pairs `(d, m)` with `d m ≤ N` in two ways (Dirichlet's *hyperbola*
  bookkeeping).
* **Multiplicativity of divisor sums.** If `p` is prime and `p ∤ m`, the divisors of `pᵃ m` are
  the `pⁱ e` with `i ≤ a`, `e ∣ m`; hence `Σ_{d ∣ pᵃm} f(d) = Σ_{i ≤ a} Σ_{e ∣ m} f(pⁱ e)`.
* **The von Mangoldt function** `Λ(n) = log p` if `n = pᵏ` (`k ≥ 1`), `0` otherwise, and the
  identity `Σ_{d ∣ n} Λ(d) = log n`, which is unique factorisation written additively. We define
  `Λ` as a double sum over pairs `(p, k)`; then sums `Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n) g(n)` regroup at once into
  sums over prime powers.

All sums are the finite sums `gsum f N = f 0 + ⋯ + f (N−1)` of Part II, over any field.

# Chebyshev's `ψ` and Mertens' estimate `Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n)/n = log N + O(1)`

Euler (1737) proved that `Σ 1/p` diverges — the analytic form of the infinitude of primes.
Mertens (1874) made this quantitative: `Σ_{p ≤ x} log p / p = log x + O(1)`. The weighted form
with the von Mangoldt function,

  `log N − 1 ≤ Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n)/n ≤ log N + log 1024`,

is proved here by the classical route through `log N!`:

1. `Σ_{d ∣ n} Λ(d) = log n` (unique factorisation, via `log n = Σ_p vₚ(n) log p`);
2. summing over `n ≤ N` and counting multiples: `log N! = Σ_{d ≤ N} Λ(d) ⌊N/d⌋`
   (Chebyshev's identity, a weighted Legendre formula);
3. `N log N − N ≤ log N! ≤ N log N` (from `Nᴺ/N! ≤ eᴺ`, a single term of the exponential series);
4. **Chebyshev's bound** `ψ(N) = Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n) ≤ π(N) log N ≤ N log 1024`, from the upper bound
   of the previous file `Chebyshev`.

Replacing `⌊N/d⌋` by `N/d` costs at most `ψ(N)`, which gives both bounds. In particular
`Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n)/n → ∞`: this is the case `q = 1` of Dirichlet's theorem in Mertens' form, and
the model for the general case, where the sum is restricted to `n ≡ a (mod q)`.

We also bound two error terms needed later: the contribution of the prime powers `pᵏ` with
`k ≥ 2` (at most `4`), and that of the primes dividing a fixed `q` (at most `2q`).

# Dirichlet `L`-series at `s = 1`

For a Dirichlet character `χ` modulo `q`, Dirichlet's `L`-series is `L(s, χ) = Σ χ(n)/nˢ`. For the
proof of his theorem only the point `s = 1` matters, and there the series converges — though not
absolutely — whenever `χ` is not the principal character. The reason is cancellation: over each
period the values of `χ` sum to `0`, so the partial sums `Σ_{n<N} χ(n)` stay bounded (by `q`),
and **Abel's summation by parts** (1826) converts bounded partial sums and decreasing weights
`b(n) → 0` into convergence of `Σ χ(n) b(n)`, with an explicit tail bound:

  `|Σ_{M ≤ n < K} χ(n) b(n)| ≤ 2 q b(M)`.

Applied to `b(n) = 1/n` this gives the number `L(1, χ)` together with
`|L(1, χ) − Σ_{n<M} χ(n)/n| ≤ 2q/M`; applied to `b(n) = log n / n` (decreasing from `n = 4` on,
because `e ≤ 4`) it shows that the partial sums of `Σ χ(n) log n / n` — the series of `−L'(1, χ)` —
stay bounded. These two facts feed the key identity of the next file.

Complex sequences converge when their real and imaginary parts do (Part II); completeness of the
reals provides the limit.

# Two small error terms: higher prime powers, and primes dividing `q`

The von Mangoldt function charges `log p` not only to the primes `p` but to all prime powers
`pᵏ`. When we finally count primes `p ≡ a (mod q)` we must check that the powers with `k ≥ 2`
contribute only a bounded amount to `Σ Λ(n)/n`:

  `Σ_{pᵏ ≤ N, k ≥ 2} log p / pᵏ ≤ 4`.

Summing the geometric series in `k` leaves `≤ 2 Σ_p log p / p²`, and `Σ_{n ≥ 1} log n / n² ≤ 2`
follows by telescoping against `(2 + log n)/n`, using `log (n+1) − log n ≤ 1/n`.

Similarly, the prime powers `pᵏ` with `p ∣ q` — exactly those `n` with `Λ(n) ≠ 0` that the
principal character modulo `q` discards — contribute at most `2q`, since
`Σ_{k ≥ 1} log p / pᵏ ≤ 2 log p / p ≤ 2` and there are at most `q` such primes.

# Twisted Chebyshev sums `Σ_{n ≤ N} χ(n) Λ(n)/n`

The prime-counting device of the whole proof is the sum

  `S_χ(N) = Σ_{n ≤ N} χ(n) Λ(n) / n`,

the "logarithmic derivative" `−L'/L(1, χ)` cut off at `N`. Dirichlet's sieve (file
`DirichletCharacters`) turns these into the sum over one residue class:

  `Σ_χ conj χ(a) · S_χ(N) = φ(q) · Σ_{n ≤ N, n ≡ a (q)} Λ(n)/n`.

For the principal character, `S_{χ₀}(N)` is Mertens' sum with the finitely many primes dividing
`q` removed, so it is at least `log N − 1 − 2q`. For the other characters we prove the **key
identity**

  `Σ_{n ≤ N} χ(n) log n / n = Σ_{d ≤ N} χ(d) Λ(d)/d · Σ_{m ≤ N/d} χ(m)/m`,

which is `log n = Σ_{d ∣ n} Λ(d)` summed against `χ(n)/n` (with `χ(dm) = χ(d)χ(m)`). The left
side is bounded (file `LFunction`); on the right the inner sums are `L(1, χ)` up to an error
`2q d/N`, and `Σ Λ(d)/d · 2qd/N = 2q ψ(N)/N` is bounded by Chebyshev. Hence

  `|L(1, χ) · S_χ(N)| ≤ 4 + 2q + 2q log 1024`,

so **if `L(1, χ) ≠ 0` then `S_χ(N)` stays bounded** — the analytic heart of the argument,
which reduces Dirichlet's theorem to the non-vanishing of `L(1, χ)`.

# Dirichlet's theorem, conditional on `L(1, χ) ≠ 0`

This file assembles the pieces into the reduction that Dirichlet himself made in 1837:

> *If `L(1, χ) ≠ 0` for every non-principal character `χ` modulo `q`, then for every `a` coprime
> to `q` there are infinitely many primes `p ≡ a (mod q)`.*

Indeed, by the sieve, `φ(q) · Σ_{n ≤ N, n ≡ a} Λ(n)/n = Σ_χ conj χ(a) S_χ(N)`. The principal
character contributes at least `log N − 1 − 2q` (Mertens), and each of the other characters a
bounded amount (since `L(1, χ) ≠ 0`, file `ChebyshevSums`). So `Σ_{n ≤ N, n ≡ a} Λ(n)/n → ∞`.
If there were only finitely many primes `p ≡ a`, all below `N₀`, this sum would be at most
`N₀ + 4`: the primes contribute `log p / p ≤ 1` each, and the higher prime powers at most `4`
(file `PrimePowers`). This contradiction proves the theorem — given the non-vanishing, which is
the subject of the next files.

# The Möbius function

The **Möbius function** (Möbius 1832; the notation `μ` is Mertens') is `μ(n) = (−1)^k` if `n` is
a product of `k` distinct primes, and `μ(n) = 0` if some square of a prime divides `n`. It is
the inverse of the constant function `1` for Dirichlet convolution:

  `Σ_{d ∣ n} μ(d) = 1` if `n = 1`, and `0` if `n > 1`,

which is the inclusion–exclusion principle in arithmetic form. Combined with
`Σ_{d ∣ n} Λ(d) = log n` it gives the inverse relation `Σ_{d ∣ n} μ(d) log d = −Λ(n)`. Both are
proved by peeling off one prime: the divisors of `pᵃ m` (`p ∤ m`) are the `pⁱ e` with `e ∣ m`,
and only `i = 0, 1` contribute, with `μ(p e) = −μ(e)`.

These identities let us *invert* `L(1, χ)` in the next file: they are the elementary shadow of
`1/L(s, χ) = Σ μ(n) χ(n) n⁻ˢ` and `−L'/L(s, χ) = Σ Λ(n) χ(n) n⁻ˢ`.

# `L(1, χ) ≠ 0` for characters that are not real

Suppose `L(1, χ) = 0` for a non-principal character. Inverting `L(1, χ)` with the Möbius
function shows that then the twisted Chebyshev sum is *large and negative*:

  `S_χ(N) = −log N + O(1)`.

Indeed `Σ_{d ∣ n} μ(d) log (N/d) = log N · [n = 1] + Λ(n)`, so summing against `χ(n)/n` gives

  `log N + S_χ(N) = Σ_{d ≤ N} μ(d) χ(d) log(N/d) / d · Σ_{m ≤ N/d} χ(m)/m`,

and if `L(1, χ) = 0` each inner sum is a tail of the series, of size `≤ 2qd/N`; the total is at
most `(2q/N) Σ_{d ≤ N} log (N/d) = (2q/N)(N log N − log N!) ≤ 2q`.

Now if `χ` is **not real**, then `χ̄ ≠ χ` and `L(1, χ̄) = conj L(1, χ) = 0` as well. But the sum of
all the `S_ψ(N)` over the characters is `φ(q) Σ_{n ≡ 1} Λ(n)/n ≥ 0`, while the principal character
contributes at most `log N + O(1)`, the two characters `χ, χ̄` contribute `−2 log N + O(1)`, and
every other character `O(1)` or less. For large `N` the total would be negative — a contradiction.
So a vanishing `L(1, χ)` can only come from a *real* character; that case needs a different idea
(next file).

# Real characters: the divisor sums `r(n) = Σ_{d ∣ n} χ(n)` and the sum `Σ r(n)/√n`

For a **real** character `χ` (values `0, ±1`) the argument used for complex characters breaks
down: `χ̄ = χ`, so a zero of `L(1, χ)` would be counted only once. The classical way out
(Mertens 1897, simplified by many since) looks at the divisor sums

  `r(n) = Σ_{d ∣ n} χ(d)`.

Because `χ` is completely multiplicative, `r(pᵃ m) = (1 + χ(p) + ⋯ + χ(p)ᵃ) · r(m)` for `p ∤ m`;
with `χ(p) ∈ {−1, 0, 1}` each factor is `≥ 0`, and `≥ 1` when `a` is even. Hence

  `r(n) ≥ 0` for all `n`, and `r(k²) ≥ 1`.

(In modern terms, `ζ(s) L(s, χ)` is the zeta function of a quadratic field and has non-negative
coefficients.) Consequently the sum `T(N) = Σ_{n ≤ N} r(n)/√n` grows at least like
`Σ_{k ≤ √N} 1/k ≥ log √N`. On the other hand, counting the pairs `(d, m)` with `dm ≤ N`,

  `T(N) = Σ_{d ≤ N} χ(d)/√d · U(N/d)`,   `U(K) = Σ_{1 ≤ m ≤ K} 1/√m`,

which the next file shows to be `2√N · L(1, χ) + O(1)`. So `L(1, χ) = 0` is impossible.

# `L(1, χ) ≠ 0` for real characters

We finish the argument begun in `RealCharacters`. Let `χ ≠ χ₀` be real and suppose
`L(1, χ) = 0`. Take `N = M²`. In

  `T(N) = Σ_{d ≤ N} χ(d)/√d · U(⌊N/d⌋)`,   `U(K) = Σ_{1 ≤ m ≤ K} 1/√m = 2√K + V(K)`,

where `V(K)` is non-increasing with values in `[−2, 0]` (compare the sum with `∫ dt/√t`):

* the **tail** `d > M` is a sum of `χ(d)` against the non-increasing weights `U(N/d)/√d`, so by
  Abel summation it is at most `2q · U(M)/√(M+1) ≤ 4q`;
* in the **head** `d ≤ M`, the main term `2M Σ_{d ≤ M} χ(d)/d` is `2M` times a tail of the series
  for `L(1, χ) = 0`, hence at most `4q`; replacing `√⌊N/d⌋` by `M/√d` costs at most `2/M` per
  term, `2` in all; and `Σ χ(d) V(N/d)/√d` is again handled by Abel summation, since
  `d ↦ V(⌊N/d⌋)` is monotone and bounded.

So `T(M²)` stays bounded, while `T(M²) ≥ log (M + 1)` because `r(n) ≥ 0` and `r(k²) ≥ 1`. This
contradiction shows `L(1, χ) ≠ 0`.

# Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions

> **Theorem (Dirichlet, 1837).** If `a` and `q ≥ 1` are coprime, there are infinitely many
> primes `p ≡ a (mod q)`.

Euclid's argument gives infinitely many primes; variants of it (file `PrimesMod4`) handle a few
progressions such as `4k + 1` and `4k + 3`, but no purely algebraic trick is known that works for
every progression. Dirichlet's proof was the first to bring analysis — infinite series, limits,
and the group characters of `(ℤ/qℤ)ˣ` — to bear on a question about whole numbers, and it is
usually counted as the birth of **analytic number theory**. He was inspired by Euler's proof
(1737) that `Σ 1/p` diverges, which is the case `q = 1`. Our `mertens_lower`,
`Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n)/n ≥ log N − 1`, is the case `q = 1` of Dirichlet's theorem in Mertens' form;
it gives the divergence of `Σ log p / p`, which is weaker than Euler's `Σ 1/p = ∞`.

The proof formalised in this part follows the elementary route through the values `L(1, χ)`:

1. `Characters`, `DualGroup`, `DirichletCharacters` — characters of finite abelian groups,
   orthogonality, Dirichlet characters and the sieve for one residue class;
2. `ArithmeticFunctions`, `Mertens`, `PrimePowers` — divisor sums, the von Mangoldt function,
   Chebyshev's bound and Mertens' estimate;
3. `LFunction` — convergence of `L(1, χ) = Σ χ(n)/n` by Abel summation;
4. `ChebyshevSums`, `DirichletConditional` — the key identity, and the reduction of the theorem
   to `L(1, χ) ≠ 0`;
5. `Mobius`, `NonVanishingComplex` — `L(1, χ) ≠ 0` for non-real `χ` (by counting zeros);
6. `RealCharacters`, `NonVanishingReal` — `L(1, χ) ≠ 0` for real `χ` (positivity of
   `Σ_{d ∣ n} χ(d)` and the hyperbola method).

This file puts them together. Everything is proved from the axioms of Lean's logic, with reals

# Toward the prime number theorem I: finite sums and logarithms

The **prime number theorem** says that the number `π(x)` of primes up to `x` is asymptotic to
`x / log x`: the ratio `π(x) log x / x` tends to `1`. Gauss, as a teenager in 1792, noticed in
tables of primes that their density near `x` is about `1 / log x`; Legendre (1798, 1808) proposed
the similar formula `x / (log x − 1.08366)`. Chebyshev (1852) proved by elementary means that the
ratio stays between two positive constants (see `Chebyshev`), and Riemann's memoir of 1859
showed that the finer question is governed by the complex zeros of the zeta function. The
theorem was proved in 1896, independently by **Hadamard** and **de la Vallée Poussin**, using the
theory of functions of a complex variable — above all the fact that `ζ(s)` has no zeros on the
line `Re s = 1`.

For half a century it was believed that no proof could avoid complex analysis: the theorem
seemed to "know" about the zeros of `ζ`. In 1948 **Atle Selberg** found an elementary
"symmetry formula", and **Paul Erdős** and Selberg then derived the prime number theorem from it
without any complex analysis (Selberg's own paper and the joint use of Erdős's ideas led to a
well-known priority dispute; both published proofs in 1949, and Selberg's Fields Medal of 1950
cited this work). "Elementary" here does not mean easy — it means using only real numbers,
limits and the logarithm. Philosophically the result was a lesson about *purity of method*:
what a theorem is "about" does not dictate which tools are needed to prove it, and an apparently
deep dependence on one branch of mathematics can turn out to be an artefact of the first proof.

The files `PNT*` follow the elementary route as far as it goes in this development. This first
file only gathers tools: identities for finite sums `Σ_{k<n} a(k)` (exchanging a double sum,
picking out a single term, counting multiples), and inequalities for the logarithm
(`log y ≤ y − 1`, and the crude Stirling-type bounds `n log n − n ≤ log n! ≤ n log n`).

# Toward the prime number theorem II: Chebyshev's functions θ and ψ

Counting primes one by one, as `π(x)` does, turns out to be awkward. Chebyshev's insight (1850s)
was to *weight* each prime by its logarithm:

* `θ(x) = Σ_{p ≤ x} log p` — the logarithm of the primorial `x#`;
* `ψ(x) = Σ_{pᵏ ≤ x, k ≥ 1} log p` — the same, but every prime power `pᵏ` also counts, with
  weight `log p`.

The second is the more natural: `ψ(x) = Σ_{n ≤ x} Λ(n)`, where **von Mangoldt's function**
`Λ(n)` is `log p` if `n` is a power of the prime `p` and `0` otherwise. The point of the
weighting is that `Σ_{d ∣ n} Λ(d) = log n` — unique factorisation, written additively — so that
`log n! = Σ_{d ≤ n} Λ(d) ⌊n/d⌋`, the identity driving the next files. The prime number theorem
becomes the statement `ψ(x) ∼ x`: the primes, weighted by their logarithms, have density one.

In this file (for natural numbers `N`):

* `Λ`, `θ`, `ψ`, and the identity `ψ(N) = Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n)`;
* `θ(N) ≤ ψ(N) ≤ π(N) · log N ≤ N · log 1024`, and `θ(N) ≤ N · log 4` from Erdős's primorial
  bound — so θ and ψ are `O(N)`;
* `ψ(N) − θ(N) ≤ √N · log N`: higher prime powers are rare, since only primes `p ≤ √N` have a
  square below `N`.

Sums over prime powers are written as double sums over pairs `(p, k)`; for a prime `p` the
number of exponents `k ≥ 1` with `pᵏ ≤ N` is `ppCount p N`, the integer part of
`log N / log p`.

# Toward the prime number theorem III: three equivalent forms

The prime number theorem can be stated in three ways, and this file proves that they are
equivalent:

  `π(N) · log N / N → 1`   ⇔   `θ(N) / N → 1`   ⇔   `ψ(N) / N → 1`.

The first is Gauss's and Legendre's conjecture — the primes up to `N` number about `N / log N`.
The last is the form in which the theorem is actually *proved*, both in the complex-analytic
proofs of Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin (1896) and in the elementary proof of Selberg and
Erdős (1949): `ψ` is the function that interacts well with multiplication, through
`Σ_{d ∣ n} Λ(d) = log n`.

* `ψ ↔ θ`: the difference `ψ(N) − θ(N) ≤ √N · log N` (previous file) is `o(N)`, because
  `log N` grows more slowly than any power of `N` — here we only need `log m ≤ 2√m`.
* `θ ↔ π`: trivially `θ(N) ≤ π(N) log N`. Conversely, cutting at `M = ⌊N/k⌋`, the primes in
  `(M, N]` each contribute at least `log M ≥ log N − log 2k`, and there are at most
  `π(M) ≤ M log 1024 / log M` primes below `M` (Chebyshev). So
  `π(N) log N − θ(N) ≤ (log 1024 / k) · N + π(N) log 2k`, and the right side is at most `εN`
  once `k` is large and then `N` is large (since `π(N) ≤ N log 1024 / log N` and
  `log N → ∞`). This replaces the usual partial summation `π(x) = θ(x)/log x + ∫ θ(t)/(t log² t)`.

The statements are about sequences indexed by natural numbers `N`, with limits in the sense of
Part II (`Tendsto`).

# Toward the prime number theorem IV: Mertens' theorems

Franz **Mertens** proved in 1874, by elementary means, that the primes are distributed "on
average" exactly as the prime number theorem predicts, when weighted by `1/p`:

  `Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n)/n = log N + O(1)`   and   `Σ_{p ≤ N} log p / p = log N + O(1)`.

These are much weaker than `ψ(N) ∼ N` (they would follow from it by partial summation, but not
conversely), yet they are the foundation of every elementary approach, including Selberg's.

The proof rests on one identity and one estimate.

* **The identity** `log N! = Σ_{pᵏ ≤ N} ⌊N/pᵏ⌋ · log p`, i.e. `log N! = Σ_{d ≤ N} Λ(d) ⌊N/d⌋`.
  It combines unique factorisation in additive form, `log m = Σ_p vₚ(m) log p`, with
  **Legendre's formula** `vₚ(N!) = Σ_k ⌊N/pᵏ⌋` from the `Binomial` file.
* **The estimate** `N log N − N ≤ log N! ≤ N log N` (a crude form of Stirling's formula, from
  `N! ≤ Nᴺ` and `Nᴺ/N! ≤ eᴺ`).

Replacing `⌊N/d⌋` by `N/d` costs at most `Σ_{d ≤ N} Λ(d) = ψ(N) ≤ N log 1024` (previous files).
Dividing by `N`: `−1 ≤ Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n)/n − log N ≤ log 1024`.

For the second theorem one removes the higher prime powers: their contribution
`Σ_p Σ_{k ≥ 2} log p / pᵏ ≤ Σ_p log p / (p(p−1))` is bounded by `2`, by comparison with the
telescoping sum of `(2 + log n)/n`.

# Toward the prime number theorem V: the Möbius function and divisor sums

Selberg's formula needs one more classical tool: **Möbius inversion** (Möbius, 1832; the
function `μ` already appears implicitly in Euler). The **Möbius function** is

  `μ(n) = (−1)ᵏ` if `n` is a product of `k` distinct primes, and `μ(n) = 0` if `p² ∣ n` for
  some prime `p`.

Its defining property is `Σ_{d ∣ n} μ(d) = [n = 1]`: summing `μ` over the divisors of any
`n > 1` gives zero, because the divisors with and without a given prime `p` cancel in pairs
`d ↔ p d`. This makes `μ` the inverse of the constant function `1` under *Dirichlet convolution*
`(f ∗ g)(n) = Σ_{d ∣ n} f(d) g(n/d)`, so that `F = f ∗ 1` can be solved for `f = F ∗ μ`.

Applied to `log = Λ ∗ 1` (unique factorisation: `Σ_{d ∣ n} Λ(d) = log n`), inversion gives

  `Λ(n) = Σ_{d ∣ n} μ(d) log(n/d) = −Σ_{d ∣ n} μ(d) log d`,

the identity that will feed the Tatuzawa–Iseki form of Selberg's argument.

We define `μ(n)` as a product of local factors `∏_{q ≤ n prime} m_q(n)` with `m_q(n) = 1, −1, 0`
according as `v_q(n) = 0, 1, ≥ 2`; then `μ(pm) = −μ(m)` for `p ∤ m` and `μ(pm) = 0` for `p ∣ m`
are factor-by-factor computations with the valuations of the `Binomial` file.

# Toward the prime number theorem VI: the Tatuzawa–Iseki identity

Selberg's own derivation of his formula (1949) inverted the function `Λ(n) log n + (Λ ∗ Λ)(n)`
with the Möbius function directly. A tidier route, due to **Tatuzawa and Iseki** (1951), packages
the inversion once and for all in an identity about arbitrary functions: if

  `G(x) = log x · Σ_{n ≤ x} F(x/n)`,

then

  `F(x) log x + Σ_{n ≤ x} Λ(n) F(x/n) = Σ_{d ≤ x} μ(d) G(x/d)`.

The left side is "Selberg-shaped"; the right side is a Möbius average of `G`. One applies it to
two functions `F₁ = ψ` and `F₂(x) = x − c` whose `G`'s nearly agree, so that the difference of the
right sides is small, and reads off the asymptotics of the left side.

We prove the identity for an integer `x = N`, with the values `F(N/n)` given as an arbitrary
sequence `Φ(n)` (this covers both `ψ(⌊N/n⌋)` and `N/n − c`): with
`Γ(d) = log(N/d) · Σ_{n ≤ N/d} Φ(dn)` (here `Φ(dn)` plays the role of `F(x/(dn))`),

  `Σ_{d ≤ N} μ(d) Γ(d) = Φ(1) log N + Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n) Φ(n)`.

The proof reorganises the double sum over `d·n ≤ N` as a sum over `m = dn` and its divisors
(the **hyperbola reindexing**), and then uses `Σ_{d ∣ m} μ(d) = [m = 1]` and
`Σ_{d ∣ m} μ(d) log d = −Λ(m)` from the previous file.

# Toward the prime number theorem VII: estimates for Selberg's formula

To apply the Tatuzawa–Iseki identity we need three classical estimates, each sharper than the
crude bounds used for Mertens' theorems:

* **Euler's constant.** `H(M) = 1 + 1/2 + ⋯ + 1/M = log M + γ + O(1/M)`. The sequence
  `H(M) − log M` decreases, `H(M) − log(M+1)` increases, and they differ by
  `log(1 + 1/M) ≤ 1/M`; so both converge to a common limit `γ` (Euler 1734; `γ ≈ 0.5772`) and
  `0 ≤ H(M) − log M − γ ≤ 1/M`. Whether `γ` is irrational is still unknown.
* **Stirling with a bounded error.** `log M! = M log M − M + ½ log M + O(1)`, here taken from the
  Stirling file of Part VIII (the sequence `log M! + M − (M + ½) log M` decreases from `1` and
  stays above `3/4`).
* **A logarithmic average.** `Σ_{d ≤ N} log²(N/d) ≤ 6N`: the sum is a Riemann sum for
  `∫₀ᴺ log²(N/t) dt = 2N`; we compare term by term with `h(t) = t (log²(N/t) + 2 log(N/t) + 2)`,
  whose derivative is `log²(N/t)`, by the mean value theorem.

We also record **Chebyshev's identity** `Σ_{n ≤ M} ψ(M/n) = log M!`, the form of
`log M! = Σ Λ(d) ⌊M/d⌋` that the Tatuzawa–Iseki identity consumes.

# Toward the prime number theorem VIII: Selberg's symmetry formula

In the spring of 1948 Atle Selberg, then at the Institute for Advanced Study, proved the asymptotic
formula

  `ψ(x) log x + Σ_{n ≤ x} Λ(n) ψ(x/n) = 2x log x + O(x)`,

equivalently `Σ_{p ≤ x} log² p + Σ_{pq ≤ x} log p log q = 2x log x + O(x)`. It is called a
*symmetry* formula because it weighs a prime `p` and the products `pq` symmetrically; heuristically
it says that the primes and the products of two primes together have exactly the density
`2 log x` they would have if `ψ(x) ∼ x`. Unlike `ψ(x) ∼ x` itself, it can be proved by
manipulating finite sums — and from it the prime number theorem follows by a delicate but purely
real-variable ("tauberian") argument. Erdős, learning of the formula, used it to prove that
`p_{n+1}/p_n → 1`; Selberg then completed a proof of the prime number theorem, and both published
elementary proofs in 1949 (Selberg in the *Annals of Mathematics*, Erdős in the *Proceedings of
the National Academy of Sciences*). How much each owed to the other became a bitter dispute,
documented in letters of the time; Selberg's Fields Medal (1950) cited this work, and Erdős
received the Cole Prize (1951) for his paper. We take no side.

Our proof follows the Tatuzawa–Iseki route (previous files). Apply the identity
`Σ_{d ≤ N} μ(d) Γ(d) = Φ(1) log N + Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n) Φ(n)` to

  `Φ(k) = ψ(⌊N/k⌋) − (N/k − c)`, with `c = γ + 1`.

On the right this gives `ψ(N) log N + Σ Λ(n) ψ(N/n)` minus
`(N − c) log N + N Σ Λ(n)/n − c ψ(N) = 2N log N + O(N)` (Mertens). On the left, with
`M = ⌊N/d⌋` and `y = N/d`, Chebyshev's identity gives
`Σ_{n ≤ M} Φ(dn) = log M! − y H(M) + cM`, and Stirling plus Euler's constant show this is
`O(log y)`; so `|Γ(d)| ≤ 4 log²(N/d) + 3`, and the logarithmic average
`Σ_{d ≤ N} log²(N/d) ≤ 6N` makes the whole left side `O(N)`.

# Toward the prime number theorem IX: Selberg's formula with `Λ ∗ Λ`

Selberg's formula is usually quoted in the form

  `Σ_{n ≤ x} Λ(n) log n + Σ_{mn ≤ x} Λ(m) Λ(n) = 2x log x + O(x)`,

in which the two kinds of "almost primes" — prime powers weighted by `log² p`, and products of
two prime powers weighted by `log p log q` — appear side by side. Writing
`(Λ ∗ Λ)(k) = Σ_{d ∣ k} Λ(d) Λ(k/d)` for the Dirichlet convolution, this file derives that form
from the `ψ`-form of the previous file. Two small steps are needed:

* `Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n) ψ(N/n) = Σ_{k ≤ N} (Λ ∗ Λ)(k)` — the hyperbola reindexing again;
* `0 ≤ ψ(N) log N − Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n) log n ≤ N log 1024` — by Abel summation the difference is
  `Σ_{j < N} ψ(j) (log(j+1) − log j)`, and each term is at most `j log 1024 · (1/j)`.

## From here to the prime number theorem

The prime number theorem `ψ(N)/N → 1` follows from Selberg's formula by the Erdős–Selberg
*tauberian* argument (in outline after Levinson's "motivated account", 1969). It is formalised in
the files that follow, using finite sums in place of integrals: `PNTRemainder` (Selberg's formula
for `R(N) = ψ(N) − N`), `PNTIterated` (`|R(N)| log² N ≤ Σ a(k) |R(N/k)| + O(N log N)`),
`PNTTauberianA`–`C` (sign changes, averaging, and the improvement lemma), and `PNTTheorem`
(`prime_number_theorem`). For comparison, the Isabelle formalisation of this proof by Avigad,
Donnelly, Gray and Raff (2007) ran to about 30 000 lines.

# Toward the prime number theorem X: the remainder `R(N) = ψ(N) − N`

The prime number theorem says that the **remainder** `R(N) = ψ(N) − N` is `o(N)`. This file
rewrites Selberg's formula in terms of `R` and collects the auxiliary facts about `R` that the
Erdős–Selberg tauberian argument (next files) needs:

* **Selberg's formula for the remainder**:
  `R(N) log N + Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n) R(⌊N/n⌋) = O(N)` — the main terms `2N log N` cancel exactly
  against `N log N + Σ Λ(n) ⌊N/n⌋ = N log N + log N!`;
* the **Selberg weights** `a(k) = Λ(k) log k + (Λ ∗ Λ)(k) ≥ 0`, with summatory function
  `A(N) = 2N log N + O(N)`, and the logarithmic average `Σ_{k ≤ N} a(k)/k ≤ log² N + O(log N)`
  (by Abel summation and `Σ log j / j ≤ ½ log² N + ½`);
* a **short-interval bound** `(ψ(n) − ψ(m)) log m ≤ 2(n − m)(log n + 1) + O(n)`: primes cannot
  crowd into an interval more than twice as densely as expected (another consequence of Selberg's
  formula, since `a(k) ≥ Λ(k) log k`);
* the **mean value** `|Σ_{n ≤ N} R(n)/(n(n+1))| ≤ B`: on average `R` is neither positive nor
  negative, which will force it to change sign in every long multiplicative interval.
